prompt: @Override public ImmutableList<UUID> load(String key) throws Exception { return externalPersisted.get(externalGroupsKeyReader.currentKey()); }
clarifying_question: The way that this is implemented now, it could race: t0: A group is added so currentKey will give a new Key next time we call it t1: The cache gets the new currentKey, it's a miss, the loader is invoked t2: A new group is added. currentKey *would* yield a different key t3: The loader is invoked, with key from t1. It will, however, now use the values from t2, so give a wrong value for the key. It's always a forward-race because at t3 (with a key of t1) we'll never have values older than t1, so not that much of an issue. But I'd like to avoid all types of races :-) One way to work around this is to define your own Key class that gets a list (TreeSet?) of Refs (in essence, that's the key) the serializer then makes a has out of that. @AutoValue GroupsExternalKey { abstract TreeSet<Ref> allGroupsRefs; static class Serializer ... { byte[] serialize(ConflictKey object) { // compute hash } public ConflictKey deserialize(byte[] in) { // We never deserialize keys. throw new IllegalStateException(); } This way, the loader can use 'allGroupRefs' to do it's work and is guaranteed to be consistent with the key. That is based on the assumption that we never deserializer keys (which I think is correct, but please check). If so, we could modify PersistedCacheDef#keySerializer to return a OneWaySerializer instead of a CacheSerializer that does not have a deserialize method. That's because we can't reconstruct allGroupsRefs from the hash. This interface change could be a follow-up to this change.

clarifying_question: I'm just being paranoid, but can we benchmark this in some common cases? Say we have: X1--X2--A \\--B A naive implementation of isMergedInto(A, B) would walk all the way from A to the root of the repo looking for B. That may be too much walking on a repo the size of Chrome. Fortunately I'm pretty sure isMergedInto is not that dumb, and it knows how to reasonbly quickly compute that the merge base of A and B is X1. But like I said, I'm being paranoid. (There's still some linear behavior if X2 is actually a string of 1000 commits, which can happen if you rebase a very old change. But I feel like the practical upper bound of the length of X2 is still much less than the upper bound of the total repo history.)
